title: Zemar Hakim
text:
Hey, glad you stopped by! I’m a PhD candidate in Economics at Queen’s University working as an applied microeconomist at the intersection of environmental, development and public economics. My research agenda studies how we can credibly identify the socioeconomic consequences of natural disasters. The first part of this agenda develops new tools using spatial data for identification. The second part provides us with evidence on how households and markets respond to these shocks, and what these responses imply for policy.
I enjoy applying quantitative tools to a variety of real-world problems. In addition to my doctorate, I have worked as a consultant for the public and private sectors. I spent the summer of 2026 as a Senior Associate Intern at Charles River Associates International, working in the Competition and Antitrust Practice in Toronto. Before that, I served as a Senior Research Analyst at Global Affairs Canada, where I applied data science to inform policy on Canada’s international economic security.
Use one of the links above to get in touch. Whether you’re curious about grad school, working as a professional economist, or just want to talk research, I’d love to hear from you.

Proximity to the Plague: Measuring Locust Exposure and Child Health


Abstract

I investigate early childhood health following the Kenyan 2020–2021 desert locust invasion by linking georeferenced locust observations to a nationally representative health survey. To account for differences in harvest times across the country, I build a treatment that conditions on the insect’s biological capacity to damage vegetation, the growth stage of the local crop, and a subsequent decline in vegetation. Children exposed in utero to locust crop damage within 30 km are 25 percent more likely to be wasted than unexposed children. Among crop-growing households, the harm is concentrated in farming zones rather than those that also rely on herding or fishing, and among children born before the lost harvest. This pattern suggests that households cut consumption in anticipation of lost food. Relief may therefore be most effective if it reaches farming households as soon as crop damage is recorded, through fast-paying instruments such as cash transfers or expanded safety nets, rather than after the harvest fails.

Wildfire smoke, air quality, and the limits of short-run labor-market impacts in Canadian cities With Christopher S. Cotton | Submitted: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences


Abstract

Wildfire-smoke-driven increases in fine particulate matter raise hours worked and employment in Canada’s nine largest metropolitan areas. This response is consistent with productivity impairment requiring longer hours to meet output targets and with degraded outdoor conditions reducing the value of non-work time. Both mechanisms imply welfare losses that standard labour-market statistics record as gains, suggesting output-based damage assessments understate the costs of smoke in urban economies.

Drought-Proof Generosity: Index Insurance and Informal Livestock Lending in Northern Kenya Last updated: April, 2026


Abstract

I investigate whether formal insurance contracts crowd out informal risk-sharing arrangements that underpin livelihoods in developing economies. Using panel data from pastoralist households in Marsabit, northern Kenya, I instrument insurance uptake with randomly distributed price discount coupons and interact coverage with sub-location drought severity. Drought erodes informal support for uninsured households. A one-standard-deviation worsening of drought lowers the probability that an uninsured household receives a livestock gift by 11 percentage points and a cash or in-kind transfer by 12 points, and lowers the probability that it gives a transfer by 11 points. Livestock borrowing does not fall. Two-stage least squares estimates suggest that the same worsening of drought raises livestock borrowing by roughly 40 percentage points more for insured than uninsured households. In the reduced form, coupon recipients also give and receive more transfers as drought deepens. I find no evidence that insurance crowds out informal risk sharing, and suggestive evidence that it helps keep informal networks active during a drought.

title: Research

Work in Progress
Born into Drought: Early-Life Exposure and Child Health in Angola


Abstract

Abstract
Drought is widely expected to harm early childhood health, yet credible causal estimates remain scarce. Observational studies typically link child outcomes to moisture indices measured at survey-cluster locations, which are displaced for confidentiality and may poorly capture the water deficit each household actually experiences. Such measurement error, together with the endogeneity of where and when households are exposed, complicates interpretation of existing estimates. This paper explores a strategy for identifying the causal effect of early-life drought exposure on child stunting in Angola, using pooled DHS surveys from 2015-16 and 2023-24 that span the 2018-2021 southern African drought. I use low-frequency oscillations in atmospheric circulation, specifically the Southern Annular Mode, as a source of plausibly exogenous variation in moisture conditions, and I evaluate how alternative instrument definitions and exposure windows (in utero, first year, second year, and cumulative) affect the strength of the first stage. The project is a work in progress: I document the relevance and limitations of this approach, discuss threats to the exclusion restriction, and assess whether circulation-driven variation can improve on standard observational measures of drought exposure. The goal is to inform the targeting and timing of nutrition and water, sanitation, and hygiene interventions in drought-prone regions of southern Africa.

Policy Papers and Other Contributions
Patent Monetization Promotion and SSO Participation With Charles River Associates


Project Details

Simcoe and Zhang (2021) study whether standard setting organizations’ intellectual property rights (IPR) policies affect participation and innovation, using two natural experiments: the W3C’s 2003 shift to royalty-free licensing and the IEEE’s 2015 revision of its patent policy. Across both settings, they find little evidence that stricter IPR terms reduced participation by standard-essential patent (SEP) licensors or innovation in patent-intensive areas, though their IEEE analysis covers only a short post-revision window. This paper extends the IEEE portion of their study — working-group contributions, organization-level contributions, and CPC-level patent applications — through 2025. The organization-level result remains a precisely estimated null over the longer window. Two other results diverge from the original findings: 802.11’s relative contribution growth becomes larger, other patent-intensive working groups now show a significant relative decline, and CPC groups more exposed to declared 802.11 patents show significantly higher post-2015 patenting. We argue these diverging results are more plausibly explained by the coincident Wi-Fi 6/6E and Wi-Fi 7 technology cycle than by the policy itself, and conclude that our extension does not overturn Simcoe and Zhang’s (2021) central finding.

G7 Sanctions Gap Analysis With Global Affairs Canada | Presented during Canada’s G7 Presidency


Project Details

This project compiled sanctions data for all five jurisdictions (US, UK, EU, Japan and Canada), recording for each affected product code and listing the specific legal citation (e.g., executive order, EU regulation article, or UK/Canada equivalent) authorizing the restriction, alongside indicators for whether the measure is an import restriction, export restriction, or listed persons. The resulting harmonized dataset allows for consistent measurement of the scope and overlap of allied sanctions regimes across countries. The report and associated analysis proivdes a foundation for measuring and understanding coordination (or divergence) toward Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the effectiveness of these measures in restricting bilateral trade flows.
